questions.prompt: For an op-amp with input currents \(I_{B1}\) and \(I_{B2}\), how are the input bias current \(I_B\) and the input offset current \(I_{OS}\) defined?
options: \(I_B=\dfrac{I_{B1}+I_{B2}}{2}\) (the average) and \(I_{OS}=|I_{B1}-I_{B2}|\) (the mismatch)
questions.explanation:
Reader Eqs. 18.1–18.2. These are DC currents the input transistors need (often BJT base currents, \(I_C/\beta\)). \(I_{OS}\) is typically about 10× smaller than \(I_B\).
They are NOT caused by a finite input resistance: they flow even with both inputs at 0 V.

questions.prompt: An op-amp's inputs draw \(I_{B1}=110\ \mathrm{nA}\) and \(I_{B2}=90\ \mathrm{nA}\). What is the input offset current \(I_{OS}\), in nA?
questions.explanation: \(I_{OS}=|I_{B1}-I_{B2}|=|110-90|=20\ \mathrm{nA}\). (The bias current is the average, 100 nA.)

questions.prompt: In the circuit shown (inverting configuration, signal input grounded through \(R_1\), \(+\) input grounded), \(R_2=1\ \mathrm{M\Omega}\) and \(I_{B1}=100\ \mathrm{nA}\) flows into the inverting input. Ignoring \(V_{os}\), what is \(v_o\), in V?
questions.explanation: \(V^-\approx0\) (virtual ground, \(V^+=0\)), so no current flows in \(R_1\). The bias current must come from the output through \(R_2\): \(v_o=0+I_{B1}R_2=100\ \mathrm{nA}\times1\ \mathrm{M\Omega}=0.1\ \mathrm{V}\) (reader Eq. 18.3).

questions.prompt: To cancel the effect of the bias currents, a resistor \(R_3\) is placed between the \(+\) input and ground. With \(R_1=10\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) and \(R_2=100\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\), what value of \(R_3\) cancels equal bias currents, in kΩ?
questions.explanation:
The reader shows \(V_o=0\) for \(I_{B1}=I_{B2}\) when \(R_3=\dfrac{R_2}{1+R_2/R_1}=R_1\parallel R_2\) (Eq. 18.6).
\(R_3=\dfrac{10\times100}{110}=9.091\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\): both inputs then see the same DC resistance to ground.

questions.prompt: With \(R_3=R_1\parallel R_2\) in place and \(R_2=100\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\), the bias currents differ by \(I_{OS}=10\ \mathrm{nA}\). What is the magnitude of the remaining output offset, in mV?
questions.explanation: With the matched \(R_3\), only the mismatch remains: \(|V_o|=I_{OS}R_2=10\ \mathrm{nA}\times100\ \mathrm{k\Omega}=1\ \mathrm{mV}\), about 10× better than \(I_BR_2\) (reader Sec. 18.2.5).

questions.prompt: Why does \(R_3=R_1\parallel R_2\) cancel the effect of equal bias currents?
options: \(R_3\) blocks the bias current from flowing
\(R_3\) changes the signal gain so that the offset is divided out
\(R_3\) makes the op-amp's input impedance infinite
\(I_{B2}\) through \(R_3\) makes \(V^+=-I_BR_3\); feedback copies it to \(V^-\), which pulls exactly the right current through \(R_1\) to offset \(I_{B1}\) in \(R_2\)
questions.explanation:
Both inputs then see the same DC resistance (\(R_1\parallel R_2\) on the inverting side, \(R_3\) on the other), so equal currents produce equal input voltages and the op-amp sees no difference. The bias currents still flow; their effects cancel. \(R_3\) carries no signal current, so the ideal gain is unchanged.
Sign note: with currents defined INTO the inputs, \(v_o=I_{B1}R_2-I_{B2}R_3(1+R_2/R_1)\). Reader Eqs. 18.4 and 18.6 have the opposite overall sign (inconsistent with Eq. 18.3), but the cancellation condition is the same.

questions.prompt: In the uncompensated circuit (\(+\) input grounded), \(v_o=I_{B1}R_2\). If \(R_1\) is changed from \(10\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) to \(1\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) (with \(R_2\) fixed), what happens to the bias-current output offset?
options: It grows 10×, like the signal gain
It shrinks 10×
Nothing: \(R_1\) has 0 V across it (both ends at ground potential), so it carries no bias current
It doubles
questions.explanation: \(V^-\approx V^+=0\) and the other end of \(R_1\) is grounded, so the bias current can only come through \(R_2\) from the output. The output offset \(I_{B1}R_2\) doesn't depend on \(R_1\) (unlike the offset-voltage error, which scales with \(1+R_2/R_1\)).

questions.prompt: A non-inverting amplifier (\(R_1=10\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\), \(R_2=90\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\)) is driven from a sensor with \(100\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) source resistance (signal set to 0 V). Both inputs draw \(I_B=100\ \mathrm{nA}\) (into the op-amp). What is the output offset, in mV (with sign)?
questions.explanation:
The \(+\) input current flows through the source resistance: \(V^+=-I_BR_s=-10\ \mathrm{mV}\), amplified by \(1+R_2/R_1=10\): \(-100\ \mathrm{mV}\). The \(-\) input current flows through \(R_2\): \(+I_BR_2=+9\ \mathrm{mV}\).
Total \(v_o=-91\ \mathrm{mV}\). Gotcha: the SOURCE resistance multiplied by the noise gain dominates. Making \(R_1\parallel R_2=R_s\) would cancel it.

questions.prompt: A student argues: 'An op-amp with infinite input resistance can't have an input bias current.' What's wrong?
options: Nothing: infinite input resistance means zero bias current
Bias current is a DC current the input devices need to operate (for example a BJT base current), not current through an input resistance, so it exists even with \(R_{in}=\infty\)
Bias current only flows at high frequency
Bias current is the same thing as offset voltage
questions.explanation: The reader stresses that the bias current is a DC current, not due to the input impedance (Sec. 18.2.3); it's modeled as current sources at the inputs of an ideal op-amp. CMOS-input op-amps have tiny bias currents (pA) because MOS gates draw almost none, not because of the input resistance number on the datasheet.

questions.prompt: Preview of datasheets. An op-amp's datasheet gives \(I_B=80\ \mathrm{nA}\). In an uncompensated inverting stage, the bias-current output error \(I_BR_2\) must stay below 1 mV. What is the largest \(R_2\), in kΩ?
questions.explanation: \(R_2\le\dfrac{1\ \mathrm{mV}}{80\ \mathrm{nA}}=12.5\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\). Datasheet specs directly limit resistor values; a CMOS op-amp with pA bias current would allow MΩ resistors.

questions.prompt: Preview of datasheets. To shrink bias-current errors you use small resistors: \(R_1=1\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\), \(R_2=10\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) in a non-inverting stage. At \(v_o=5\ \mathrm{V}\), how much current must the op-amp output supply into the feedback network alone, in mA?
questions.explanation: The output drives \(R_2\) in series with \(R_1\) to ground: \(I=\dfrac{5\ \mathrm{V}}{11\ \mathrm{k\Omega}}=0.455\ \mathrm{mA}\). Smaller resistors mean more output current and power, which is why the reader notes that lower \(R_2\) needs a higher-power op-amp; the datasheet's output-current spec bounds this trade.

questions.prompt: Preview of noise. Resistors in the feedback network convert the op-amp's input currents into voltage errors. Which design choice reduces BOTH DC bias-current errors and (as you'll see) the random noise contributed by the feedback resistors?
options: Using smaller resistor values (at the cost of more output current)
Using larger resistor values
Adding a capacitor in series with \(R_2\)
Increasing the supply voltage
questions.explanation: Bias error \(\approx I_BR_2\) scales with resistance. Resistor thermal noise also grows with \(R\) (\(v_n\propto\sqrt{R}\)), and noise currents turn into voltages through the same resistors. The reader notes low-noise designs favor small feedback resistors.
